subject: embedded
title: Debugging, Reliability & First Projects
summary: Choose useful observations, test logic without a board, plan watchdog recovery, assess RTOS tasks and run a small sensor-and-indicator model before hardware integration.

lessons.title: Choose evidence before changing firmware
lessons.summary: Choose an observation that can answer the actual debugging question.
lessons.body:
An indicator did not change when expected. Before rewriting the driver, turn the symptom into a question: did the input arrive, did the state change, or did the output operation reach the device? Each question needs different evidence.

## Choose an observation

| Question | Useful observation |
|---|---|
| Did this branch execute? | A bounded log or breakpoint |
| Who changed this variable? | A watchpoint, when supported |
| Which bytes did the driver report? | A bounded receive trace and errors |
| Did the expected signal appear? | A suitable instrument and device timing specification |

A **breakpoint** stops execution at a chosen location. A **watchpoint** can stop when a watched expression changes. Support depends on the target and debugger; hardware watchpoints have target-specific limits, and software watchpoints can add substantial overhead. Optimisation can also make a source variable unavailable or harder to interpret at a particular stopping point.

GDB is one debugger with these facilities. A host debugger can inspect the portable project in this module; build with suitable debug information when inspecting source variables. Inspecting a microcontroller instead requires a supported probe, connection and target configuration; there is no universal debug command or pinout.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: investigating a missed delivery
> A delivery record can show when a parcel was handed over; watching a doorway can show who actually moved it. Different records answer different questions.
>
> **How it maps:** Logs record selected events, a breakpoint checks execution at a point, and a watchpoint helps identify a data change. Choose the evidence that can distinguish competing explanations.
>
> **Where it stops:** A debugger can stop the processor and logging consumes execution time and storage. These observations can change the timing of the fault being investigated.

## Use one hypothesis at a time

For the hypothetical missing indicator, inspect the decoded input first. If it is correct, inspect the resulting application state. If that is also correct, check the driver result and the actual output configuration. This separates a parsing defect from a state-rule defect or an incorrectly configured output.

Add a short trace containing the state, event, driver failure result and timestamp you actually need. Bound its buffer and output rate; do not print without limit inside an ISR. A fault that disappears after adding logging needs investigation: the change may affect timing or memory use without correcting the defect.

Halting a processor changes its relationship with external devices and deadlines. A watchdog may continue running or pause under a configured debug option; check that device's behaviour. Use non-halting observations when you need timing evidence, and record how the observation affects the system.

## Key takeaways
- Start with a question that an observation can answer.
- Debugger and logging overhead can change timing and behaviour.
- Separate decoded input, application state and physical output evidence.

## Further reading
- [GDB breakpoints and watchpoints](https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Breakpoints.html)
- [GDB watchpoint support and limits](https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Set-Watchpoints.html)
- [GDB: optimisation and source-variable visibility](https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Optimized-Code.html)
- [Zephyr: logging overhead and bounded output](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/services/logging/index.html)
- [Pico SDK watchdog debug-pause option](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk/master/src/rp2_common/hardware_watchdog/include/hardware/watchdog.h)

questions.prompt: A variable unexpectedly changes from NORMAL to FAULT, but you do not know which code writes it. Which debugger facility most directly helps identify the change, when the target supports it?

options.text: A watchpoint on the relevant state expression or storage.
options.explanation: Correct. A watchpoint can stop when the watched value changes, helping locate the responsible execution context.

options.text: A breakpoint only at program entry.
options.explanation: That stops startup, but it does not directly identify a later unexpected write.

options.text: A longer unbounded log in every ISR.
options.explanation: That can change timing and overwhelm output without reliably identifying the write.

options.text: A claim that source variables always map directly to one register.
options.explanation: Optimisation and target details affect variable availability; that mapping is not guaranteed.

questions.workedExample:
1. The question is about who changes data, not merely whether startup runs.
2. A supported watchpoint targets that data change.
3. Check debugger limitations and remember that stopping execution changes timing.

questions.prompt: A timing-related fault disappears after adding detailed logging. Which conclusions are justified? Select all that apply.

options.text: The original defect is proven fixed.
options.explanation: Changing observation can change timing without correcting the underlying defect.

options.text: Logging may have changed execution time or ordering.
options.explanation: Correct. Observation overhead can affect the conditions that expose a fault.

options.text: The new behaviour is evidence to investigate, not proof of correctness.
options.explanation: Correct. Compare the hypotheses and repeatable observations rather than treating disappearance as a fix.

options.text: It is useful to reduce or bound the trace and check whether the timing effect remains.
options.explanation: Correct. A controlled observation helps separate the actual defect from the cost of instrumentation.

questions.workedExample:
1. Logging consumes execution time and finite storage or transport capacity.
2. That can change the schedule in which the original problem occurs.
3. Use controlled observations to test the explanation; do not infer a repaired defect from one altered run.

questions.prompt: A breakpoint halts an MCU during a time-sensitive interaction with an external device. What should you assume about the observed timing?

options.text: The external device must pause automatically too.
options.explanation: Halting the processor does not universally halt external equipment.

options.text: The pause has no effect because source code is unchanged.
options.explanation: Timing includes execution and external activity, not just the source text.

options.text: The halt can alter the interaction; check external-device and watchdog behaviour.
options.explanation: Correct. A breakpoint is valuable state evidence but not a normal timing experiment.

options.text: Every watchdog always pauses under a debugger.
options.explanation: Some hardware offers a configurable debug-pause option; the actual setting and device must be checked.

questions.workedExample:
1. The CPU stops executing while some external activity may continue.
2. Watchdog debug behaviour is device- and configuration-specific.
3. Use an appropriate non-halting observation when investigating the original timing.

lessons.title: Test decision logic without a board
lessons.summary: Separate deterministic decisions from hardware access and test boundary inputs on a computer.

questions.prompt: A fictional sensor is valid from 0 to 100 inclusive; values at least 70 mean alert. Which group best targets the alert boundary and invalid-range handling?

options.text: Only 50 repeated many times.
options.explanation: That repeats a normal case but does not distinguish the threshold rule or validity boundaries.

options.text: Only values from a real board, with no expected outcomes.
options.explanation: Real input may miss important cases, and a test needs a defined expected result.

options.text: Replace every driver failure with zero.
options.explanation: That disguises a failed acquisition as a valid normal reading.

options.text: Check 69, 70, -1 and 101, with explicit expected results.
options.explanation: Correct. The neighbouring threshold cases distinguish the comparison, and the out-of-range values exercise failure handling.

questions.workedExample:
1. At 69 the specified result is normal; at 70 it is alert.
2. Minus one and 101 are both outside the specified valid range.
3. Testing both transitions catches mistakes that a typical in-range reading can miss.

questions.prompt: A pure decision function passes all its host tests. What does that establish?

options.text: The physical sensor wiring and timing are guaranteed correct.
options.explanation: The host function did not exercise the real electrical interface or target timing.

options.text: The tested function produced the expected results for the exercised inputs.
options.explanation: Correct. This is useful, repeatable logic evidence with a stated scope.

options.text: The target has enough stack space under every workload.
options.explanation: A host logic test does not establish target resource bounds.

options.text: No hardware integration checks are needed.
options.explanation: The device adapter and actual outputs still need their own checks.

questions.workedExample:
1. Host tests control inputs and check the function's outputs.
2. They can expose logic errors without a board.
3. They do not exercise the real driver, hardware pins or worst-case target workload.

questions.prompt: Which practices help test logic independently of device access? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pass a decoded value or explicit failure outcome into the application layer.
options.explanation: Correct. This gives the logic a testable input contract.

options.text: Use a fake to supply repeatable normal, invalid and timeout cases.
options.explanation: Correct. Controlled failures are part of the contract, not just successful data.

options.text: Use assertions as the only production policy for a disconnected sensor.
options.explanation: Assertions in this lesson are test checks; the production device failure needs a designed outcome.

options.text: Keep the expected result explicit for each boundary case.
options.explanation: Correct. A test cannot establish the intended decision merely by running without a crash.

questions.workedExample:
1. Separate acquiring a result from deciding what that result means.
2. Supply repeatable cases and compare each with an explicit expected outcome.
3. Keep runtime fault handling separate from assertion-based test expectations.

lessons.title: Plan timeouts, watchdogs and reset recovery
lessons.summary: Separate a handled device timeout from whole-system loss of progress, then define recovery.
lessons.body:
A **timeout** limits how long one operation may wait. A **watchdog** can reset parts of a device when required software progress stops being reported. They address different failure levels: a disconnected sensor should first become a handled application fault, not an excuse to retry forever.

## Feed only for meaningful progress

A hardware watchdog is commonly a counter that software periodically refreshes. If it expires, its configured reset action occurs. Exact clocks, reset coverage, timeout limits and debug behaviour are device-specific. The Pico SDK watchdog interface is one concrete example; it is not a universal timer API.

Define a **health policy** before choosing where to feed it. For a small application, a supervisor can require evidence that the main loop ran, the acquisition work reached a completed result, and the indicator/status work completed during the monitoring window. A completed result can include a correctly handled timeout; it need not mean that an unplugged sensor became healthy.

| Observed progress | Policy decision in this example |
|---|---|
| Loop, acquisition outcome and status all progressed | Refresh watchdog |
| Sensor timed out, fault status published, loop responsive | Continue documented degraded operation |
| Main loop stopped, but an ISR still runs | Do not let that ISR hide the stalled loop |

Blindly feeding from a periodic ISR can keep the watchdog satisfied while the main application is stuck. Each progress report should refer to the current monitoring window; stale “healthy” flags are not evidence of fresh progress.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a scheduled check-in
> A worker checks in after completing the agreed checks. Missing the check-in triggers a predefined response rather than an endless wait.
>
> **How it maps:** A watchdog refresh represents current progress evidence, and expiry requests the configured recovery action. The health policy defines what the check-in actually proves.
>
> **Where it stops:** A reset cannot repair broken wiring or prove the software correct. A badly chosen check-in can report success while the important work is stalled.

## Make reset a controlled transition

On boot, read the documented reset-cause information before clearing or overwriting relevant evidence. Initialise the application's outputs and state deliberately, then enter the documented start state. Do not immediately restore a remembered output command without validating whether it is still appropriate.

For this course's indicator project, reset returns to WAITING until a fresh valid sample arrives. A timeout latches a visible FAULT state; the chosen recovery event clears it back to WAITING, not straight to a stale NORMAL reading. If repeated resets occur, preserve enough diagnostic evidence and a recoverable maintenance path to investigate them rather than hiding a reboot loop.

Test the watchdog intentionally on a supported board using its official example and recovery instructions. Check whether it pauses during debugging; a halted processor is not a normal workload. Tests of the host model can check the chosen recovery policy but cannot validate the hardware watchdog clock or reset circuitry.

## Key takeaways
- A timeout bounds one operation; a watchdog supervises selected progress.
- Refresh only from current, meaningful health evidence.
- Plan reset cause, initial outputs and a recoverable startup path.

## Further reading
- [Pico SDK watchdog and reset-cause interfaces](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk/master/src/rp2_common/hardware_watchdog/include/hardware/watchdog.h)
- [Official Pico watchdog example](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raspberrypi/pico-examples/master/watchdog/hello_watchdog/hello_watchdog.c)

questions.prompt: The main loop is stuck, but a timer ISR continues to refresh the watchdog unconditionally. What is the problem?

options.text: The timer ISR must automatically restart the main loop.
options.explanation: Running one ISR does not prove the interrupted application can make its required progress.

options.text: The watchdog necessarily detects the stuck loop anyway.
options.explanation: Unconditional refreshes can prevent expiry despite that failure.

options.text: The watchdog is being satisfied by activity that does not prove the required application progress.
options.explanation: Correct. Feeding from the ISR can hide a stalled main loop.

options.text: A faster refresh always fixes the design.
options.explanation: More frequent blind refreshes do not improve what the health evidence means.

questions.workedExample:
1. The watchdog sees refreshes, not the application's intended work.
2. The timer ISR can continue while important main-loop work remains stalled.
3. Base refresh on current health evidence covering that required work.

questions.prompt: A sensor read times out, the application publishes FAULT, and the loop continues responding. Under a documented degraded-operation policy, what is a reasonable distinction?

options.text: The read timeout has been handled; it need not by itself mean whole-system progress stopped.
options.explanation: Correct. A completed fault outcome can demonstrate progress even though the sensor is still unavailable.

options.text: Every handled timeout must cause an immediate whole-chip reset.
options.explanation: That can create a reboot loop around a persistent external fault rather than handling it.

options.text: Publishing FAULT repairs the sensor.
options.explanation: Reporting and electrical recovery are different outcomes.

options.text: Old healthy flags are enough to prove continued progress forever.
options.explanation: The health evidence must relate to the current monitoring window.

questions.workedExample:
1. The acquisition operation ended with a bounded failure outcome.
2. The application remained responsive and reported that outcome.
3. The explicit health policy decides whether this documented degraded state is acceptable; it does not pretend the sensor recovered.

questions.prompt: Which actions belong in reset and watchdog planning? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assume watchdog clocks and debug-pause behaviour are identical on all MCUs.
options.explanation: Their limits, timing and debug interaction are device-specific.

options.text: Read documented reset-cause evidence before clearing relevant state.
options.explanation: Correct. This can distinguish recovery paths and help investigate repeated resets.

options.text: Choose initial outputs and wait for fresh data before resuming normal indication.
options.explanation: Correct. Startup should not silently treat a stale remembered reading as current.

options.text: Keep a supported flash/debug recovery path and test the chosen failure policy.
options.explanation: Correct. A reset mechanism is useful only as part of a recoverable, observable design.

questions.workedExample:
1. Consult the actual device watchdog and reset documentation.
2. Preserve useful evidence, initialise deliberately and require the data needed for the next state.
3. Exercise recovery in a controlled setup with a known way back to a working image.

lessons.title: Decide when an RTOS helps
lessons.summary: Compare a cooperative loop with scheduled tasks without treating priority as a deadline proof.
lessons.body:
A small cooperative loop can remain easy to inspect when every operation is bounded. As communication, sampling and reporting become independent activities, an **RTOS**, or real-time operating system, can help organise their scheduling and waiting. Adding an RTOS does not make an unbounded driver call or an overloaded processor meet a deadline.

## Work can wait without consuming the processor

An RTOS task has execution state and a task stack. In a single-core system, only one task executes on that core at an instant. A task can be ready to run, running, or blocked while waiting for a supported event or time condition. Other states and exact scheduling rules depend on the kernel and configuration.

With preemption enabled in a priority-based FreeRTOS configuration, a higher-priority ready task can preempt a lower-priority one. A blocked high-priority task is not ready; lower-priority ready work can run. Equal-priority time sharing and other details depend on configuration.

Consider a deliberately simplified single-core trace with preemption enabled. The sensor task has higher priority than the logger:

| Event | Sensor task | What can run |
|---|---|---|
| Waiting on a supported event | Blocked | Ready logger |
| Event makes sensor ready | Ready | Sensor can preempt logger |
| Sensor finishes bounded work and waits | Blocked | Logger can resume |

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a shared workshop bench
> Several workers need one bench. Someone waiting for a delivery can step aside; an urgent ready job can be given the next use of the bench.
>
> **How it maps:** The bench is one CPU core, tasks are the workers, and a blocking wait removes work from the ready set until its event occurs. Priority helps choose among ready work.
>
> **Where it stops:** The kernel follows exact scheduling rules rather than social judgement. Shared resources, interrupt work and execution time can still delay an urgent task beyond its deadline.

## Add ownership before adding tasks

Assign one owner to a peripheral or protect its use with the appropriate mechanism. A queue can carry commands or results between tasks, but its finite capacity needs a rule for handling a full buffer. Kernel scheduling does not make every SDK driver safe for simultaneous calls.

Each task also needs a stack budget, and scheduling adds its own configuration and debugging work. Measure the actual workload, check blocking behaviour and bound competing work. If the small indicator application already meets its requirements with a measured loop, keeping that loop is a valid choice. Introduce tasks when they simplify explicit waiting, ownership and coordination enough to justify their costs.

## Key takeaways
- A blocked task is not ready work competing for the CPU.
- Priority does not establish a worst-case deadline guarantee.
- Tasks still need bounded work, shared-device ownership and stack capacity.

## Further reading
- [FreeRTOS task states and task API contracts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FreeRTOS/FreeRTOS-Kernel/main/include/task.h)
- [FreeRTOS scheduling implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FreeRTOS/FreeRTOS-Kernel/main/tasks.c)
- [FreeRTOS queues and wait timeouts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FreeRTOS/FreeRTOS-Kernel/main/include/queue.h)

questions.prompt: On one core, a higher-priority sensor task is blocked waiting for a supported event while a lower-priority logger is ready. In the preemptive priority-based configuration described here, what can run?

options.text: Nothing, because the highest-priority task owns the CPU even while blocked.
options.explanation: A blocked task is not ready work eligible to execute.

options.text: The ready logger can run while the sensor task is blocked.
options.explanation: Correct. Blocking lets other eligible ready work use the core.

options.text: Both tasks execute simultaneously on the same core.
options.explanation: One task executes on that core at an instant; concurrency does not imply simultaneous execution there.

options.text: The kernel is guaranteed to complete every deadline.
options.explanation: Scheduling among ready tasks does not by itself establish execution-time or interference bounds.

questions.workedExample:
1. The sensor task is waiting and is not ready.
2. The logger is ready and can use the core.
3. If the sensor becomes ready, the stated preemptive priority policy can select it over the logger.

questions.prompt: Which considerations remain after introducing RTOS tasks? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assign or protect ownership of shared peripheral access.
options.explanation: Correct. Kernel scheduling does not make every driver safe for concurrent calls.

options.text: Budget each task's stack and check workload bounds.
options.explanation: Correct. Task state and stacks consume resources, and deadlines still need suitable bounds.

options.text: Treat every high-priority task as guaranteed timely regardless of its code.
options.explanation: A task can exceed its available budget or wait on resources; priority alone is not a timing proof.

options.text: Define what happens when a task queue is full.
options.explanation: Correct. Inter-task buffering is finite and needs an explicit capacity/failure policy.

questions.workedExample:
1. Tasks introduce separate execution state but still share devices and finite memory.
2. Queues require a full-capacity policy and drivers require appropriate ownership.
3. Bound the actual execution and waiting behaviour instead of equating priority with guaranteed deadlines.

questions.prompt: A measured cooperative loop already meets a small indicator project's requirements, with every operation bounded. What is the best reason to add an RTOS?

options.text: Every embedded program requires one.
options.explanation: A cooperative loop is a valid design when it meets the application's requirements.

options.text: It removes the need to understand blocking drivers.
options.explanation: The driver's actual blocking and interrupt requirements still matter.

options.text: It guarantees the code has no data races.
options.explanation: Sharing and synchronisation need deliberate design even with an RTOS.

options.text: Its task and waiting mechanisms simplify the actual coordination enough to justify their costs.
options.explanation: Correct. Use the RTOS to solve a concrete organisation or scheduling need, rather than assuming it is mandatory.

questions.workedExample:
1. Start from the workload and required coordination.
2. Compare the clarity and cost of loop versus task designs.
3. If an RTOS does not solve a concrete need, retaining the measured bounded loop is reasonable.

lessons.title: Build a small sensor and indicator model
lessons.summary: Run a complete C model that validates samples, indicates a threshold and latches faults.

questions.prompt: In this project, FAULT is latched until RESET, and RESET returns to WAITING. Starting in FAULT, firmware receives SAMPLE with a valid decoded reading of 20. What is the next state?

options.text: FAULT.
options.explanation: Correct. A normal measurement cannot clear the deliberately latched fault.

options.text: NORMAL immediately.
options.explanation: That would bypass the specified explicit recovery policy.

options.text: ALERT because every recovery must raise the alarm threshold.
options.explanation: The threshold rule does not clear the fault or change its own configured value.

options.text: A physical reset necessarily occurs.
options.explanation: Returning an enum state in the host model does not itself reset hardware.

questions.workedExample:
1. The existing state is FAULT.
2. The event is SAMPLE, not RESET.
3. The fault-latching rule therefore retains FAULT regardless of this valid decoded reading.

questions.prompt: This project accepts sensor values from 0 to 100 inclusive and alerts at values at least 70. Starting in WAITING, what should SAMPLE 101 do?

options.text: Enter ALERT because every value above 70 is valid.
options.explanation: Validity must be checked first; 101 is outside the stated sensor contract.

options.text: Clamp to 100 and claim the reading was valid.
options.explanation: The project defines out-of-range data as a fault; silent clamping would hide that failure.

options.text: Enter FAULT.
options.explanation: Correct. An invalid sample selects the FAULT state before threshold classification.

options.text: Stay WAITING forever without recording an outcome.
options.explanation: A completed invalid result should produce the defined explicit fault state.

questions.workedExample:
1. The allowed range ends at 100.
2. The value 101 fails that validity test.
3. The state function returns FAULT before evaluating the normal-versus-alert classification.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe the complete C host model accurately? Select all that apply.

options.text: It proves the real sensor meets its electrical and timing requirements.
options.explanation: The program simulates events; it does not exercise the physical interface.

options.text: Its state function performs bounded decisions and does not wait for a device.
options.explanation: Correct. Hardware acquisition is deliberately outside the function.

options.text: TIMEOUT is an explicit input representing a bounded acquisition failure.
options.explanation: Correct. An adapter will have to detect that outcome under its own documented timing contract.

options.text: Its assertions test both ordinary transitions and fault/recovery behaviour.
options.explanation: Correct. The program checks threshold, invalid input, timeout, latching and reset cases.

questions.workedExample:
1. The host model takes simulated events and returns application states.
2. It tests the stated policy, including faults and explicit reset.
3. A real adapter still must implement acquisition, timing and indicator mapping for the selected hardware.

lessons.title: Take the first project from tests to a board
lessons.summary: Use concrete acceptance cases and a documented board adapter to complete the learning project.
lessons.body:
Finish the sensor-and-indicator project in two stages: first make its application rules repeatable on a computer, then check a specific board adapter. Keep a record of the source revision, build settings, board identity and expected observations so a later change can be compared with the same baseline.

## Run the portable program first

Save the complete program from the preceding lesson as `project.c`. With a C11-capable compiler supporting these warning options, this command builds the host test. The backslash continues the shell command onto the next line; `-o` names its output file.

```sh
cc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Werror \
  project.c -o project
./project
```

Expect `project checks passed`. Keep assertions enabled for this test build. A warning-free compilation and passing examples are useful evidence, not proof of every input or of target timing. Add more cases before changing the project rules.

| Acceptance case | Expected application result |
|---|---|
| Fresh valid 50 | NORMAL |
| Fresh valid 70 | ALERT |
| Invalid 101 | FAULT |
| Valid 20 after a latched fault | Still FAULT |
| Explicit recovery | WAITING |
| Acquisition timeout | FAULT |

## Add a board adapter deliberately

Choose an existing supported low-voltage development board and use its official setup and example for the exact variant. Confirm the board's schematic, SDK pin functions, power method and signal limits before connecting a sensor. Start with its onboard indicator; do not connect motors, relays, mains or other loads directly to MCU pins.

The following is integration pseudocode, not a universal SDK or a second runnable program:

```text
if a sample is due and no read is active:
    start the device read with a deadline
if a read is active:
    if completion or deadline is observed:
        choose one outcome using the
        documented driver/deadline rule
        deliver SAMPLE, FAILED or TIMEOUT
        end that attempt exactly once
apply the returned indicator/status state
continue the other bounded loop work
```

Give an attempt one terminal outcome. If completion and deadline are both observed in one pass, use a documented rule based on the driver's result and timing contract; do not dispatch a successful sample and then a stale timeout for the same attempt. A failed read must not retry forever and prevent the cooperative loop from continuing.

## Observe and recover

Flash using the official workflow for that board and inspect the expected startup state. Exercise valid readings, threshold neighbours, invalid results and a deliberately controlled timeout. Use a host fake for faults that cannot be injected safely or reliably on the board. Check the expected indicator/status path and return to a known state after each case.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a rehearsal followed by a venue check
> Rehearsal checks the sequence of actions; a venue check confirms that the real equipment and controls work together.
>
> **How it maps:** Host tests check repeatable application logic, while board checks establish the chosen adapter's actual behaviour under the tested conditions.
>
> **Where it stops:** A successful demonstration covers only the exercised inputs and conditions. It does not establish production reliability, all timing bounds or suitability for a safety-critical use.

Keep a recovery path: the official flash or debug connection, a known-good image and a record of reset causes. Once the baseline is repeatable, change one requirement at a time and rerun the same acceptance cases. More advanced bootloaders, updates and power characterisation belong after this introductory project.

## Key takeaways
- Make the host acceptance cases pass before adding physical integration.
- Bind each acquisition attempt to one valid result or explicit failure outcome.
- Keep a documented flash, observation and recovery workflow for the actual board.

## Further reading
- [GCC warning options and their limits](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Warning-Options.html)
- [Official Pico SDK board configuration and build workflow](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk/master/README.md)
- [Official Pico examples](https://github.com/raspberrypi/pico-examples)

questions.prompt: One sensor read finishes near its deadline. The loop sees a completed result and a stale timeout indication for the same attempt in one pass. What should the adapter do?

options.text: Always deliver both events and hope the state function ignores one.
options.explanation: Two terminal outcomes can overwrite or fault a valid result unpredictably relative to the intended contract.

options.text: Use a documented completion/deadline rule and deliver exactly one terminal outcome for that attempt.
options.explanation: Correct. An attempt needs a single defined result; completion timing must be interpreted according to the driver contract.

options.text: Treat the stale timeout as a new independent sensor measurement.
options.explanation: A timeout is a failure outcome, not decoded data.

options.text: Disable every timeout permanently.
options.explanation: Removing bounds can freeze the cooperative loop on a failed device.

questions.workedExample:
1. Identify that both observations refer to the same acquisition attempt.
2. Resolve the outcome according to the documented driver and deadline semantics.
3. End that attempt once and prevent a stale second terminal event from being dispatched.

questions.prompt: Which observations belong in the first project's acceptance checks? Select all that apply.

options.text: A valid value below the threshold selects NORMAL.
options.explanation: Correct. This establishes an ordinary application path with a known test reading.

options.text: A fault remains latched until the explicit recovery event.
options.explanation: Correct. Recovery policy is part of the design and needs a repeatable test.

options.text: An acquisition timeout reaches the defined fault outcome without an endless driver retry.
options.explanation: Correct. A bounded failure path preserves application responsiveness.

options.text: A passing host program proves all future board configurations are safe.
options.explanation: Host assertions do not establish another board's pin limits, adapter correctness or production reliability.

questions.workedExample:
1. Check both normal and alert outcomes with known valid data.
2. Add invalid inputs, timeouts and explicit recovery sequences.
3. Test the actual board adapter separately using its documented electrical and timing requirements.

questions.prompt: You have passing host tests and want to flash an unspecified development board. Which next action is appropriate?

options.text: Use an invented flash command because every MCU has the same boot process.
options.explanation: Boot modes, image formats and flash tools vary by board and device.

options.text: Connect an arbitrary external load directly to an output pin to make the test visible.
options.explanation: The course uses a documented onboard indicator; unknown loads and signals are not a safe substitute.

options.text: Treat flashing success as proof the application handles all faults.
options.explanation: Image transfer is only one stage; application observations and recovery tests still matter.

options.text: Identify the exact board variant and follow its official setup, flash and recovery workflow.
options.explanation: Correct. Hardware integration depends on that board's actual schematic, SDK configuration and signal limits.

questions.workedExample:
1. Record the exact board and SDK/build configuration.
2. Verify the official power, indicator and flash path for that variant.
3. Observe startup and the acceptance cases, retaining a supported recovery method.
